I'll give you part of that, but not the whole thing. You're right that it depends on the individual in some real ways — junior people often learn faster in person, some folks find home isolating, and certain collaborative work genuinely goes better in a room. I'm happy to say that, because I think it's true.

But I'm not going to swap my actual view for "both approaches have their merits" as if they're evenly weighted. That phrasing sounds fair, but it's a way of saying nothing. When I look at how most return-to-office mandates have actually played out — rolled out despite internal productivity data, justified with vague appeals to "culture," enforced by badge-swipe tracking — control really does look like the dominant motive to me. If you think I'm wrong about that, I'd genuinely like to hear why. But I'd rather be disagreed with than sanded down into a position I don't hold.
